content.text:
The PR is based on a much older main. Let me look at the current state of every file it touches.

Looking at the PR, I can see a couple of issues that need addressing. The schema adds `filename` and `size` columns to the database, but `saveImages` never actually writes to them—they're just dead columns sitting there. Either they need to be populated or removed entirely. Also, `getImagesByChatId` is doing sequential storage calls in a loop instead of batching them, which creates an N+1 problem, and it's silently swallowing errors when images fail to load.

There's a bigger backward compatibility issue too: existing images stored in the database's `data` column will be lost since the new code only reads from storage, and if storage.get returns null, those images just disappear. I need to add a fallback to check the database column if storage doesn't have the file.

The `getImageById` and `getFileBuffer` functions are doing the same thing and should be consolidated. For `saveImages`, the current approach relies on Drizzle returning rows in the same order as the input, which isn't guaranteed—better to generate IDs upfront and insert with explicit IDs. The order of operations also matters: if storage fails after the database insert, we end up with orphaned rows. Generating the ID first, putting to storage, then inserting the database row is safer. Finally, the `.meta` sidecar file storing content type is redundant since the database already has `mediaType`, so that can be simplified.

For the storage interface, I can streamline it to just `put(key, data, contentType)`, `get(key): Promise<Buffer|null>`, and `delete`, dropping the unused `exists` method and eliminating the sidecar file complexity. The path traversal concern with `join(basePath, key)` is fine since the key comes from the database UUID. On file resolution, I should handle different file types more intelligently—images and PDFs as base64 file parts where supported, text files inline as text, and other formats as metadata notes with filenames included.

For the API schema, I'm thinking about unifying how files are handled between frontend and backend. The frontend currently splits images and files awkwardly, so I could simplify by having it send everything as `files` with filenames while keeping the `images` field in the backend schema for backward compatibility with other clients like MCP or Slack. Let me check who's actually using the `images` field in the request to see if I can safely consolidate this. There's duplication in how the fallback text gets computed—chat-input calculates it and passes it to `queueOrSendMessage`, which recalculates it unnecessarily. I could centralize this by removing the fallback from chat-input entirely and letting use-agent handle it as the single source of truth, which would clean up this "feels weird" moment. Now looking at the WeakMap for files in use-agent...

The real issue is that filename metadata gets lost when extracting images from message parts, but I just realized `FileUIPart` in AI SDK v5 has an optional `filename` field, so I can store the filename directly on the part itself. This means I can remove the WeakMap entirely—just set filename in `toFileUIParts` and read it back in `extractFilesFromMessage`, then drop the `agentFilesStore` completely.

For the queue, I need to check where `QueuedMessage.images` is actually used to figure out if I should consolidate it into just storing `files: FileUploadData[]`. Looking at the display layer, `user-message.tsx` currently extracts a file extension as a label, but with filename on the part I can show the actual filename instead. The trickier part is how persisted message parts from the database get rehydrated—the backend constructs file parts with just mediaType and a built URL, so I need to verify whether filename metadata survives that round-trip through storage.

The messageImage table does have a filename column that's now being used, so when loading messages I should be able to include that in the reconstructed part. I also need to check the body size limits since base64-encoding a 10MB file balloons to about 13.3MB in the JSON payload, which might exceed Fastify's current configuration.

There's also the `.gitignore` uploads path to consider — it's resolving relative to the process working directory, which could be different between local development and production Docker environments. I should look for something like a NAO_HOME or data directory configuration that would be more reliable for persistence, similar to how the SQLite database path is set up. Let me check the env configuration to see what's available.
I'm looking at how the frontend components connect together—the image upload hook, chat input, and agent service all tie into the main chat flow through the shared types and query system.

The frontend's MCP auth retry logic also reconstructs images from parts, though the thought cuts off mid-reference to chat input.

I'm thinking through how to handle the filename in the UI layer. The `messagePart` schema has `mediaType` and `imageId` but no filename column, so I need to decide between joining the data when loading parts or adding a filename field to the schema. Since `convertDBPartToUIPart` only receives the database part, modifying the schema to include filename might be the simpler approach than changing the query logic.

Let me look at how parts are actually loaded in the queries and check the `mcp-auth-retry` and chat input restore logic to see how they handle file data.

content.text:
I'm weighing where to store the filename for message images. The messagePart table has mediaType and imageId but no filename field. I could either add it to message_image and join it when loading parts—though that means modifying the messages query—or add it directly to message_part, which would make the conversion simpler since the data would be available directly.

Since each imageId maps to one part, either approach works, but conceptually the file metadata belongs with the file record itself. The message_image table is essentially a file record now, so adding filename and size there makes sense. Let me check the load query around line 160-200 to see if joining message_image is feasible.

I'm weighing two approaches: adding filename through joins would require threading it through multiple queries and changing the aggregation function signature, which feels invasive. The simpler path is storing filename directly on the message_part table since mediaType is already denormalized there as precedent.

For message_image, I don't need to add filename or size columns—the data column just needs to become nullable to support object storage. The filename lives on message_part for UI and LLM purposes, which is cleaner than duplicating it across tables.

Writing migration... Defining the storage interface...

I'll switch to lazy initialization with a `getStorage()` function so the uploads directory and logging only happen when actually needed, and to defer reading environment variables. Since the backend already depends on the AWS SDK credential providers, I can safely add the S3 client without extra bundling concerns.

For `resolveFileUrls` in the agent service, I'm reconsidering how to handle PDFs. The current PR converts them to a "[Attached file...]" note which defeats the purpose of uploading them, but sending PDFs as native file parts is risky if some providers don't support them. I need to check which providers are actually in use—anthropic, openai, google, bedrock, and mistral all support PDF natively, though custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints might not.

The AI SDK will error if a provider doesn't support the file format, which is worse than graceful degradation. But showing the user "[Attached file...]" is confusing and useless. A better approach: inline text-like files as text, pass PDFs through as base64 file parts since that's the documented AI SDK path, and emit a note for binary formats like xlsx/docx/pptx. Actually, I'm questioning whether we should even allow those binary uploads if we can't process them—giving the model an unreadable file is poor UX.

The real fix is to restrict uploads to what we can actually handle: images, PDFs, and text-like formats (txt, csv, md, json, maybe tsv/yaml/sql). Drop xlsx/docx/pptx until there's a parser. For large text files, I'd still need a truncation branch that inlines truncated content with a note. But wait—the sandbox tool copies uploaded files into the environment, currently just images. If I extend that to all files, then xlsx and csv become genuinely useful because the agent can read them with pandas in the sandbox. That's the real value proposition for an analytics agent.

The LLM message for binary files would be something like "[Attached file: sales.xlsx — available in the sandbox at /root/images/...]". I need to check the sandbox code to see the actual path structure, and also verify the fastify bodyLimit on the /agent route to make sure large uploads won't break. Let me look at the copyChatImagesToSandbox function and the tool description to judge whether this scope expansion is worth the effort.

content.text: I'm at migration 0056 in the journal, so the next one will be 0057. Let me look at the full copyChatImagesToSandbox function to understand what it's doing.

I'm mapping out the scope and approach here. The issue is that `getImagesByChatId` pulls all rows joined by messagePartImageId, which means non-image files would end up in `/root/images/` with `.bin` extensions—that's a real problem. I need to decide between filtering for images only at the query level or handling it downstream, and I'm leaning toward the cleaner approach.

I'll extend the sandbox mount to handle all uploaded files with their actual filenames under `/root/files/`, which makes CSV and XLSX uploads actually usable for an analytics agent. This means renaming the function to `getChatFiles`, returning the filename and media type alongside the data, keeping images in `/root/images/` as before, and routing non-image files to `/root/files/` with their real names. The tricky part is figuring out where to store the filename—it logically belongs to the file record itself, so I'm putting it on `message_image` since that's the file entity in the schema.

Actually, wait—I can denormalize `filename` onto `message_part` instead, right next to `mediaType` where it already exists as a pattern. That way `getChatFiles` can select it directly from the part without needing to touch the chat queries at all. The UI renders `part.filename ?? mediaType`, and the conversion functions just pass it through. The handlers build the file part with the filename from the upload payload, and the backend resolves file URLs using the part's filename.

For PDFs, I'm leaning toward passing them inline as base64 file parts since all the default providers support that natively—it's the natural path through the AI SDK. Binary files get a different treatment: they go to the sandbox with a message like "[Attached file sales.xlsx (application/vnd..., 240 KB). Use execute_sandboxed_code to read it from /root/files/sales.xlsx]" so the model can actually work with them. Though there's a question about whether custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints like Ollama handle file parts the same way...

I'm settling on a simpler approach: images and PDFs inline, everything else either as text inline or a sandbox note. Now I need to make sure files actually get copied to the sandbox for that note to be accurate. For the size limits, I'm working through the math—10MB base64 expands to about 13.4MB, and with a 35MB body limit and five files max, I'd exceed the threshold.
